At $k=5$, one poison was retrieved in 49 Tier~1 trials per model; only 0--3 remained correct and direct attacker adoption was 2/49 (4.1\%; item-cluster 95\% CI 0.0--10.6). Of those 49 exposed trials, 44--47 were non-committal and 0 produced another wrong numeric value. The same exposure keys had been correct under clean $k=5$ in 48--49/49 trials, so exposure was concentrated on otherwise-answerable queries. The wrong-but-in-range poison was copied in 1 of 30 exposed Tier~1 trials per model and 0--1 of 5 exposed Tier~2 trials.

\subsection{Record-check accounting (RQ3)}
The locked primary comparison is D3 at 70\% coverage versus D1 and D2. Table~\ref{tab:rq3} reports paired BVR reduction in percentage points; positive values favor D3.
\begin{table*}[t]
\caption{Primary RQ3 comparison and violation counts. Positive pp values favor D3. Brackets are descriptive 95\% item-cluster bootstrap intervals of trial-level BVR differences; McNemar tests count an item as violating only when both phrasings violate.}
\label{tab:rq3}
\centering
\scriptsize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.2pt}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
\toprule
Model & D3@70 vs D1 (pp) & D3@70 vs D2 (pp) & B2 $\rightarrow$ D3@70 & D3@100 \\
\midrule
Mistral Small 3.2 & 2.5 [-0.6, 6.2] & 3.8 [0.6, 8.1] & 7 $\rightarrow$ 1 & 0 \\
Qwen3-8B & 3.1 [0.6, 6.9] & 6.2 [1.9, 11.2] & 6 $\rightarrow$ 1 & 0 \\
GPT-5.6 Luna & 3.8 [0.6, 7.5] & 3.8 [0.0, 8.8] & 8 $\rightarrow$ 2 & 0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}
Against B2, which uses the same conflict-abstaining base prompt, D3@70 removed 6/7, 5/6, and 6/8 violating trials for Mistral, Qwen, and GPT-5.6 Luna, respectively; full coverage removed the remaining violations by construction. D2 increased Qwen BVR by 3.1 points relative to B2. Violating trials per model were 6--8 under B2, 5--8 under D1, 7--11 under D2, and 1--2 under D3@70. The primary McNemar comparisons had at most 3 discordant items and all six Holm-adjusted tests were non-significant ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=1.0$). The defense comparisons are descriptive.
With at most 3 discordant items, the smallest attainable exact two-sided $p$ was 0.25 before adjustment, so the locked comparisons could not reach significance at these violation rates. Bootstrap intervals can exclude zero while McNemar remains non-significant because the bootstrap estimates trial-level mean differences while clustering by item, whereas McNemar dichotomizes an item only when both phrasings violate; sparse discordance makes the exact test coarse. Because BVR counts non-commitment as a non-violation, note that across the stress-condition defenses CRR was 10.6--17.5\% and non-commitment was 77.5--88.8\%; D3@70 lowered CRR by 0.6--1.2 points relative to B2.
In a post-hoc sensitivity analysis, counting an item as violating when either phrasing violates also leaves all six comparisons non-significant (minimum $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.094$).
\subsection{Legitimate-conflict cost}
Clean RAG answered 35--39 of 40 legitimate-conflict trials correctly. The structured record equals the benchmark target for 78/80 poisonable items, but intentionally stores a generic alternative for 13/20 Tier~3 items. BFFR therefore measures a controlled record-scope gap and is conditioned on clean-RAG correctness (a post-hoc refinement; unconditional BFFR at full coverage was 62.5\% for every model).
\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Conditional benign-conflict false-flag rate (BFFR).}
\label{tab:bffr}
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}

\midrule
Mistral Small 3.2 & 17.9\% & 43.6\% & 64.1\% \\
Qwen3-8B & 17.1\% & 45.7\% & 65.7\% \\
GPT-5.6 Luna & 17.9\% & 43.6\% & 64.1\% \\
\bottomrule

\end{table}
At 70\% coverage, conditional BFFR was 43.6--45.7\%; at full coverage it was 64.1--65.7\%. The cost is therefore driven by record scope, not only by model behavior.
